messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: Simulating non-normal ordinal data
parts:
Is it possible to simulate non-normal ordinal data with specific values of skewness and kurtosis using thresholds?

No, not by specifying the skew/kurtosis directly, since those values are calculated assuming the data are continuous.  You could do either of the following, depending on what you mean by "non-normal ordinal data"
  1. Simulate non-normal latent item responses with chosen skew/kurtosis values, then discretize them to create your ordinal "observed" item responses.
  2. Simulate data for which the normality assumption is met for the latent item responses, but choose asymmetric thresholds that make the histograms look non-normal.
(2) would require a little trial-and-error to find the skew/kurtosis values you want, by figuring out what the "mean" of the distribution would be for the ordinal items, as implied by the proportion of the population in each category.  For example, if 20% are 1s, 30% are 2s, 40% are 3s, and 10% are 4s, then the mean would be .2*1 + .3*2 + .4*3 + .1*4 = 2.4.  Then you can use the formulas found here and here to calculate the 3rd- and 4th-order moments implied by the same proportions (e.g., 20% are 1 - 2.4 = -1.4 away from the mean, 30% are 2 - 2.4 = -0.4 away from the mean, etc.).

If you want to use some thresholds from a previous simulation study, here is an example (see p. 170):

http://dx.doi.org/10.1080/10705511.2014.882658

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

  2. Simulate data for which the normality assumption is met for the latent item responses, but choose asymmetric thresholds that make the histograms look non-normal.

Hello Terry (or anyone else who may know more about this). I've always been fascinated with the idea of how to simulate ordered categorical data because if we see some sort of asymmetry in the observed proportions it could either come because the latent distribution is skewed and the thresholds are evenly-spaced OR the distribution is indeed normal but the thresholds are uneven. But, in reality, there is no way of knowing... is there? Would it make any difference to simulate data one way or the other? Say we were testing the Type 1 error rate of the chi-square test of model fit. Could one expect one method of simulating ordinal data to yield a different Type 1 error when compared to the other? Or some bias on the polychoric/tetrachoric correlations?

- Elia

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: Simulating non-normal ordinal data
parts: if we see some sort of asymmetry in the observed proportions it could either come because the latent distribution is skewed and the thresholds are evenly-spaced OR the distribution is indeed normal but the thresholds are uneven.

Correct, and it can get even more complicated.  It is possible that both are true (asymmetric thresholds AND nonnormal latent item-response).  If the latent-response distribution is nonnormal, is that because that latent common factor is nonnormal, or because the residuals are nonnormal?  Again, it could be both, especially if important 3rd variables are omitted from the model (e.g., bimodal common-factor and/or latent-response distributions due to sex differences).
But, in reality, there is no way of knowing... is there?
No, these are among the assumptions we have to make in order to draw inferences.  Regardless of the method we use, our inferences will always be conditional on "if our assumptions are met, then..."
Would it make any difference to simulate data one way or the other?

Although I have seen studies implement one or the other of these methods, I haven't seen a study directly comparing both methods. I would be interested in reading such a study, because the two methods of simulating data represent two very different real-world scenarios.  
  • Simulating normal item responses and discretizing them with asymmetric thresholds is technically not a violation of any assumption.  Thresholds are chosen from a (standard) normal distribution, so if latent item responses are normal, the assumption is met.  But in practice, more asymmetric thresholds have been shown to yield inflated Type I error rates (again, even though assumptions were met):  http://dx.doi.org/10.1080/10705511.2014.859510
  • Simulating nonnormal item responses means that the thresholds chosen from a normal distribution do not apply, even if those are the ones used to discretize the data.  The estimated thresholds will be the ones that return model-implied proportions in each response category assuming the latent response is normal, not the thresholds you actually used to simulated data.  I think this method of simulating "skewed"-looking ordinal data only makes sense if you are concerned with situations when you would not expect a normally distributed continuous response, even if you used a more sensitive measurement instrument (e.g., a 0-10 scale) that could be treated as continuous.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

parts:
Thank you for the explanation. Since second suggestion is not easy to get right, I opted for the first one.

Since you are actually analyzing the data as ordinal, I'm not sure what the goal of your study is, but different methods of simulating data represent very different implications.  Your criterion for the simulation method should reflect the situation you want to generalize to (under what conditions you want to provide researchers with advice), not the complexity of the method.  Here is a study that used many different levels of "skew/kurtosis" (see p. 105, including the footnote).

http://dx.doi.org/10.1080/10705511.2014.859510

Although she did not report the thresholds she used in each condition, you could email her for that information.  You could also use trial-and-error to generate a single huge sample (100,000) under different thresholds.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
